summary:
Obadiah is the shortest book of the Old Testament: twenty-one verses, a single vision against Edom, the nation descended from Esau, Jacob's twin (Genesis 25:24–26) — hence the charge: "violence against your brother Jacob" (v. 10). The name means "servant of the LORD"; the book says nothing else about him. Edom held mountain country southeast of the Dead Sea and trusted it: "The pride of your heart has deceived you, O dwellers in the clefts of the rocks" (v. 3) — the Hebrew for "rocks," sela, is also the name of an Edomite fortress city (2 Kings 14:7). God answers: "Though you soar like the eagle and make your nest among the stars, even from there I will bring you down" (v. 4).

The offense came on one day: foreigners entered Jerusalem's gates and "cast lots" for the city — dividing its spoils by chance — while Edom "stood aloof," gloated, plundered, and cut off fugitives at the crossroads: "you were just like one of them" (v. 11). Most interpreters connect this to Babylon's destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC; some propose an earlier raid (2 Chronicles 21:16–17); the book itself gives no date. Much of verses 1–9 closely parallels Jeremiah 49:7–22; the direction of borrowing is debated. The vision then widens to the Day of the LORD — the day God steps in to judge — for all nations: "As you have done, it will be done to you" (v. 15). Deliverance comes on Mount Zion, and the last line reads, "And the kingdom will belong to the LORD" (v. 21).
